viscose.origin: Viscose is regenerated cellulose made mostly from dissolving pulp, a highly purified wood pulp, although cotton linters can also be used. Dissolving pulp is specified by purity and reactivity; one enzyme study targeted less than 3% xylan, over 92% ISO brightness and a Fock reactivity of about 70% for viscose grades. Hardwoods such as beech and softwoods such as spruce are used, and pulping method changes the hemicellulose that remains. Man-made cellulosic fibers made up about 6% of world fiber output in 2022, and viscose is the most common of them.
viscose.structure: Chemically, viscose is cellulose again, but regenerated in the cellulose II crystal form with a lower degree of polymerization and a less ordered structure than cotton. Coagulation in an acid bath forms a skin before the core, leaving regular viscose with a serrated or lobed cross-section and fine longitudinal striations. Scanning X-ray microdiffraction shows a skin-core morphology with microfibrils about 100 nm across, built from ribbon-like elementary fibrils about 6 by 2 nm, stacked less regularly than in air-gap spun fibers. Viscose carries a few carboxyl groups, about 20 mmol/kg in one study, and a thin hemicellulose-rich surface layer.
viscose.process: Pulp is steeped in sodium hydroxide to form alkali cellulose, pressed and shredded, then aged, typically for one to two days, to lower the degree of polymerization to the target viscosity. Xanthation with carbon disulfide converts it to cellulose xanthate, which dissolves in dilute caustic soda as an orange-yellow viscous solution, the viscose. During ripening the xanthate groups redistribute among the 2, 3 and 6 positions of the glucose units and the solution becomes spinnable. After filtration and deaeration it is extruded into a sulfuric acid bath, where the cellulose regenerates and the sulfur compounds are released. Filaments are stretched, washed and finished, then cut to staple, the main form, or wound as filament.
viscose.performance: Viscose is highly absorbent, with slightly higher moisture regain than lyocell, and dyes readily with reactive and direct dyes that bind to cellulose hydroxyl groups, giving deep, bright shades. Its less ordered structure makes it weak when wet: regular viscose loses close to half its tenacity wet, so fabrics can stretch, shrink or distort in washing and are often labeled for gentle care. It drapes fluidly, creases readily and chars rather than melts. Cellulose-based knits shed more fiber fragments by mass than polyester in one laundering study, but rayon and cotton fragments biodegraded in aerobic water tests while polyester persisted.
viscose.identify: Burn tests are indicative only; viscose burns quickly like cotton, with a paper-like smell and little soft ash. The microscope is more useful: regular viscose shows longitudinal striations and a serrated cross-section, distinct from the round profile of lyocell and the twisted ribbon of cotton. FTIR confirms cellulose but not the process. Plant-source terms such as bamboo or eucalyptus describe the pulp, not a different fiber; if the cellulose was dissolved and regenerated, the fiber is still rayon or viscose.
viscose.labeling: Under 16 CFR 303.7, rayon is a manufactured fiber of regenerated cellulose in which substituents have replaced not more than 15% of the hydrogens of the hydroxyl groups. Because the rule incorporates ISO 2076, viscose is also acceptable in the United States, and modal and lyocell have their own permitted names. In the EU the name is viscose under Regulation (EU) No 1007/2011. Pulp-sourcing claims are separate from fiber-content labeling and usually rest on forest certification such as FSC or PEFC; branded lower-impact viscose, such as LENZING ECOVERO, depends on producer certificates that buyers should check.
viscose.past: The viscose process was patented in 1892 by the British chemists Charles Cross, Edward Bevan and Clayton Beadle and industrialized in the early twentieth century as artificial silk. Its solvent, carbon disulfide, soon became an occupational-health story: an Italian physician reported carbon disulfide poisoning to the 1928 international occupational health congress, and a Finnish cohort showed a 4.7-fold excess of heart-disease deaths in 1967 to 1972 that disappeared after exposures were cut. In South Korea, where rayon manufacture had been transferred from Japan, a viscose factory produced a mass poisoning in the late 1980s and closed in 1993. Studies in Chinese plants later found color-vision effects below the exposure limit.
